findings.claim: attribution biases that prevent the team from seeing systemic causes (fundamental attribution error, actor-observer bias, self-serving bias)
findings.failure_mode: concept not in deep or source, attributed to the source
findings.evidence: Deep 77-81 (Ch 3.3) names two attribution biases only: FAE and self-serving bias. Source 3931-3947: 'Two such errors, or attribution biases, should be noted here.' grep 'actor-observer' in the converted source: 0 hits. The concept is held by openstax-psychology-2e deep 277 (Ch 12.1).
findings.fix: correct: (fundamental attribution error, self-serving bias)

findings.claim: Actor-observer bias and self-serving bias. The team attributes its own difficulties to situational factors and other functions' difficulties to their character.
findings.failure_mode: concept not in deep or source, attributed to the source
findings.evidence: As D001. Only the second sentence ('Success goes to the team; failure goes to external actors') traces to the source's self-serving bias (deep 81; source 3942-3945).
findings.fix: correct: Self-serving bias. Success goes to the team; failure goes to external actors (Ch 3.3). (Actor-observer bias is held in the corpus by OpenStax Psychology 2e, Ch 12.1, not by this source.)

findings.claim: the presence of a single dissenter collapsed conformity (Ch 9.2, 'Conformity and Deviance'). In retros: written-first input before verbal discussion breaks the conformity dynamic.
findings.failure_mode: finding imported from another source, attributed to this one
findings.evidence: Deep 294 gives only the over-one-third result and three moderators (personality, stimulus ambiguity, group characteristics). Source 13870-13906 has no dissenter result (grep 'dissenter': 0 hits). The dissenter and private-response findings are in openstax-psychology-2e deep 291 (Ch 12.4).
findings.fix: correct: The Asch conformity finding: in over one-third of trials the naive subject denied the evidence of his own senses to agree with a unanimous group of confederates (Ch 9.2, 'Conformity and Deviance'). In retros: written-first input before verbal discussion gives each person a view on record before the room converges (Psychology 2e, Ch 12.4, reports that private responding and a single dissenter reduce conformity).

findings.claim: Groups prioritise cohesion over critical thinking; symptoms include self-censorship, illusion of unanimity, and suppression of minority views (Ch 6.6, 'Disadvantages of Group Decisions') ... Preventatives from OB: assign a devil's advocate, encourage everyone to speak, leaders withhold initial positions.
findings.failure_mode: another source's content attributed to this one
findings.evidence: Deep 202-204 (Ch 6.6): groupthink = members choose not to voice concerns to keep the peace; counter-measures are diverse membership, encouraging everyone to speak, a devil's advocate, finding common ground. Janis's symptom list and 'leaders withholding initial positions' are openstax-psychology-2e deep 295 (Ch 12.4), nearly word for word. grep 'illusion of unanimity', 'self-censorship' in the OB source: 0 hits.
findings.fix: correct: Groupthink "occurs when group members choose not to voice their concerns or objections because they would rather keep the peace and not annoy or antagonize others" [V]; suppression of dissent is when a more powerful member discourages differing opinions (Ch 6.6). ... Preventatives from OB: diverse membership, encourage everyone to speak, assign a devil's advocate (Ch 6.6).

findings.claim: In retros: high-performing, cohesive teams are especially at risk.
findings.failure_mode: source-supported, absent from deep; slightly strengthened
findings.evidence: Deep 202 gives no cause of groupthink. Source 8908-8914 (Ch 6.6): 'Sometimes groupthink occurs because the group has a positive team spirit and camaraderie ... It can also occur because past successes have made the team complacent.' The source says 'sometimes'; 'especially at risk' strengthens it.
findings.fix: correct: In retros: cohesive teams with a run of success can fall into groupthink: the text names team spirit and complacency from past success as causes (Ch 6.6). cycle-to-deep: source 8908-8914.

findings.claim: Big Five personality traits as contextual diagnostics. ... high conscientiousness ... high agreeableness ... high neuroticism ... (Ch 11.7).
findings.failure_mode: framework and chapter section absent from deep and source
findings.evidence: Deep 49-51 (Ch 2.4) gives the text's six work-relevant traits: self-esteem, locus of control, introversion-extroversion, authoritarianism, dogmatism, dependability. Ch 11 has five sections (source 16284-16728); there is no Ch 11.7. grep 'Big Five', 'neuroticism': 0 hits; 'agreeableness' appears once, describing transformational leaders (18892).
findings.fix: strip (or replace with the text's own traits, e.g. locus of control and dogmatism, Ch 2.4)

findings.claim: Variable-ratio schedules produce the most extinction-resistant behaviour (Ch 4.2, Table 4.2).
findings.failure_mode: table finding loosened
findings.evidence: Deep 116-123 (Table 4.2): variable interval and variable ratio both give 'slow extinction'; variable ratio gives 'very high' performance. Neither the deep nor the table ranks VR as most extinction-resistant. Source 10396-10399 (Ch 7.3) says variable-ratio schedules are 'superior' overall and fixed-interval least effective.
findings.fix: correct: Variable schedules (interval or ratio) give slow extinction, and variable ratio gives the highest performance (Ch 4.2, Table 4.2); the text calls variable-ratio schedules superior once a behaviour is learned (Ch 7.3). cycle-to-deep: source 10396-10400.

findings.claim: The retro experiment-review phase is the scheduled reinforcement that makes action-completion norms durable.
findings.failure_mode: source's schedule findings inverted
findings.evidence: A review held every sprint is a fixed-interval (time-contingent) schedule. Deep 120: fixed interval gives 'average and irregular' performance and 'quick extinction'. Deep 125 [V]: 'the performance-contingent (or ratio) reward schedules generally lead to better performance than the time-contingent (or interval) schedules'. Source 10397-10399: 'the fixed-interval schedule produces the least effective results'.
findings.fix: correct: The retro's experiment review is a regular checkpoint, but by the text's account a fixed-interval schedule alone gives quick extinction (Ch 4.2, Table 4.2); reinforcement tied to completing actions (ratio-based) holds up better (Ch 4.2; Ch 7.3).

findings.claim: "we've always done it this way" (appeal to tradition) and "everyone agrees this is the problem" (bandwagon) are the two most common fallacies that prevent the insight phase from producing a genuine root-cause analysis.
findings.failure_mode: unsupported frequency claim
findings.evidence: Deep 196 lists the seven fallacies of Table 6.2 with no frequency data; nothing ranks any as most common, in retros or elsewhere.
findings.fix: correct: ... are two fallacies from Table 6.2 that often stall the insight phase.

findings.claim: "The most cohesive teams are honest about what's not working — that's what makes them cohesive."
findings.failure_mode: script embeds a causal claim the source does not make
findings.evidence: Deep 298 (Ch 9.2) lists seven determinants of cohesiveness: homogeneity, maturity, size, frequency of interaction, clear goals, competition or external threat, prior success. Honesty about problems is not among them.
findings.fix: correct: "Strong teams can afford to be honest about what's not working. Today that's our goal."

findings.claim: Same experiment proposed but never completed | Reinforcement-schedule problem; variable-ratio schedule is maintaining the norm | Address the commitment mechanism in Phase 0.5; make follow-through scheduled, not random
findings.failure_mode: source's schedule findings inverted (recurrence of D008)

notes: Counting: claims_audited counts distinct assertions (relevance claims, key-concept sub-claims, table rows, pattern and anti-pattern items, worked-example steps, integration rows, borrowed-through items, named limits, integrity-note items); faithful = claims_audited - findings. Quote check against the converted source: the FAE definition (3937-3939) and 'can actually lead to improved performance' (8416-8417) are word for word. The SDT line ('researchers have consistently found ...') is a close paraphrase of source 10155-10156, carried [BT] against the deep's [V]; [BT] fits the source's own framing and is judged faithful. The derived-from-deep sha256 (a475cbbb...) matches the current deep ref. Main pattern: three items import openstax-psychology-2e content under OB citations (actor-observer bias D001/D002/D011; Asch single-dissenter D003/D021; Janis groupthink symptoms and 'leaders withhold initial positions' D004), and one imports a framework neither deep nor source holds (Big Five at a non-existent Ch 11.7, D006/D020). Recurring claims listed at each occurrence: actor-observer bias (D001, D002, D011); cohesion-breeds-groupthink (D005, D012, D014); scheduled reinforcement (D008, D013). Integration rows checked against other deep refs: openstax-psychology-2e (attribution 275-277, Asch 291, groupthink 295), lfuo-learning-review-guide-2024 (FAE gloss 69, sense-at-the-time framing 178-184) and nhs-just-culture-guide ('action singling out an individual is rarely appropriate', deep 15) hold; the Field Guide carries the Sprint Retrospective protocol (deep 57). Non-graded: the Worked Example carries no verbatim blockquote; Key Concept 7's '[V, paraphrased]' marker is copied from deep 298, which uses the same self-contradicting marker (deep-ref cleanup). Deep-ref gaps surfaced (cycling candidates): source 8908-8914 (causes of groupthink), 10396-10400 (Ch 7.3 schedule ranking: VR superior, FI least effective), endnote 17 at 31272 (Ryan and Deci for SDT).
